vignette: Akua had always taken pride in her independence. As a financial analyst, she was meticulous and self-sufficient, able to navigate complex spreadsheets with ease. But it wasn't until she fled war-torn Liberia at the age of 35 that Akua began to feel a creeping sense of powerlessness. The memories of those chaotic days still lingered - being forced to abandon her home, separated from her family in the chaos, and subjected to endless checks by militia groups. The natural environment seemed to hold particular menace for Akua; the sight of lush green forests or winding rivers would transport her back to those fateful days on the run. The sensation was akin to a physical blow - she'd feel winded and disoriented, as if the past had caught up with her once more. Avoiding nature became second nature: weekend hikes were abandoned in favour of solitary jogs through the city streets; even potted plants began to disappear from her apartment. Akua's relationship with authority figures also underwent a seismic shift after her displacement. The sight of police uniforms or even just their presence would send her heart racing - she'd worry about being stopped, questioned or worse still, detained. She found herself mentally rehearsing worst-case scenarios: What if they asked for my papers? What if I couldn't prove who I was? To mitigate these fears, Akua began to sidestep any situation that might involve authority figures. Grocery shopping became an online affair; dealing with customer service representatives at work turned into a high-stakes event she tried her best to avoid. The ripple effects of these anxieties soon extended far beyond the confines of her own life. Her friends and family grew increasingly worried about Akua's hypervigilance regarding their well-being - they'd receive frantic calls from her if they didn't answer within minutes, peppered with worst-case scenarios that left them both frightened and exhausted. Disagreements or confrontations became impossible for Akua to navigate; she'd freeze up at the slightest hint of conflict, convinced that things would spiral out of control. Work started to suffer too - colleagues noted a growing reluctance in Akua to contribute during meetings, especially when discussions turned contentious. Project deadlines loomed large and unmanageable as her fear of being overwhelmed took hold. The irony was not lost on Akua: the very independence she once cherished now seemed like an illusion; every move dictated by an undercurrent of anxiety. Akua's most insidious fear, though - the one that gnawed away at her in the dead of night - was that she'd lose control entirely. One wrong step and the past would catch up with her once more. And so she went through the motions: worked from home when possible, kept phone conversations to a minimum and obsessively tracked news headlines for any hint of instability. It wasn't until Akua's sister passed away after a protracted illness that she hit rock bottom - consumed by an overwhelming sense of regret for having avoided saying goodbye in person. That crushing loss made her see the full extent of how fear had hijacked her life; all those missed opportunities, abandoned connections and stifled conversations now seemed like so many chances foregone. As Akua sat in therapy, recounting fragments of her story to a quiet, compassionate listener for the first time, something shifted ever so slightly - perhaps just enough space opened up to consider that maybe control wasn't an illusion after all.
